title: The Nephilim and the giants
intro: The Nephilim appear briefly in Genesis 6:1-4 as mighty figures in the days before the flood, and Numbers 13:33 mentions them again among the inhabitants of Canaan. The Bible does not explain exactly who they were, and the Church has no defined doctrine about them. Christians have understood the passage in different ways: as descendants of Seth's line mingling with Cain's, as powerful tyrants and warriors, or, in some ancient Jewish writings, as the offspring of heavenly beings. Many Church Fathers favoured the first reading. What the text clearly stresses is the growing corruption that led to the flood.

title: Cain's wife and the first families
intro: Genesis does not name Cain's wife, but it tells us that Adam and Eve had other sons and daughters. The Church has traditionally understood that Cain married one of his sisters or other descendants of the first family, since all humanity then came from Adam and Eve. Later laws against such marriages came only after the human family had grown large. The story's real focus is not the genealogy but the first murder and God's mercy even toward Cain.

title: The Tower of Babel
intro: At Babel, people try to build a tower to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God confuses their language and spreads them across the earth. The sin is pride, trying to reach heaven by human power. The Church sees Pentecost as its answer: the Holy Spirit gathers every language into one body.

title: Adam and Eve and the Fall
intro: God creates man and woman in his image and places them in the garden in friendship with him. They choose to disobey, and sin enters the world, which the Church calls the Fall. Yet God does not abandon them; he promises a Redeemer. Catholics read the story as a true account of humanity's origin in meaning, while it can be read as a symbolic narrative in form.

title: Cain and Abel
intro: Cain's offering is not accepted, jealousy grows into anger, and he kills his brother Abel. God confronts him, protects him from vengeance, and still sends him away. The story shows how sin crouches at the door and how jealousy can become violence if we do not master it.

title: Why did God send the flood?
intro: The flood story says that violence and corruption filled the earth and that God grieved. Yet even then he saves Noah's family and starts again with a covenant. The Church sees the flood as a sign of Baptism, where sin is washed away and new life begins. Whether the flood was local or worldwide is not defined doctrine; the Church is concerned with its religious message.

title: Did God harden Pharaoh's heart?
intro: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it. The Church understands that God does not force anyone to sin; he permits Pharaoh's stubbornness to bring about his plan, and Pharaoh's free choices remain his own. The Bible often attributes to God what he allows. Notice how many times Pharaoh refuses first.

title: Why did God let Satan test Job?
intro: In Job, Satan can act only within the limits God sets. The book does not claim that God likes suffering; it shows that faith can survive when answers are not given. The Church teaches that God permits evil only to bring a greater good, and that in Christ he enters our suffering himself.

intro: King Saul, abandoned by God, secretly visits a medium and asks her to call up the dead prophet Samuel. Scripture shows God allowing Samuel to speak, but to condemn Saul. The Church forbids any attempt to contact the dead through mediums, and this story is not an example to follow.

intro: Elijah does not die; he is taken to heaven in a whirlwind with a chariot of fire, and his mantle falls to Elisha. Because of this, he returns in Jewish expectation, and Jesus says John the Baptist came in the spirit of Elijah. At the Transfiguration, Elijah appears with Moses.

title: The Annunciation
intro: The angel Gabriel greets Mary and announces that she will conceive the Son of God by the Holy Spirit. Mary, troubled and curious, asks how this can be and then answers: let it be done to me according to your word. Her yes opens the way for the Incarnation, and Catholics celebrate it on March 25.

title: The Passion and death of Jesus
intro: The Passion tells how Jesus was betrayed, arrested, condemned, and crucified, freely giving his life for our sins. Every detail is a sign of his love, from Gethsemane to the cross. Catholics enter into this mystery most deeply during Holy Week and each time we attend Mass.

title: The visit of the Magi
intro: Wise men from the East follow a star to find the newborn king, bringing gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Their visit, celebrated at Epiphany, shows that Christ came for all nations, not only Israel. Herod's fear shows how the world can react to the true King.

title: Pentecost
intro: Fifty days after Easter, the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles as wind and tongues of fire, and they begin to preach in many languages. Catholics call this the birthday of the Church. Pentecost shows that the Spirit gives courage, unity, and the power to share the Gospel.

intro: On a mountain, Jesus' face shines like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appear beside him as the Father's voice says: this is my beloved Son. The apostles glimpse his glory before the cross. It reminds us that suffering is not the final word.
